The Castilian king was free from his father's cruelty and treated her gently, but at least Henry, during the first years of their marriage, had loved his mother. She had not enjoyed that privilege for a single day, and she no longer expected Philip's feelings to change. He considered her like a sister, even though he slept with her to fulfill his duty, seeking an heir who never came. She carried a barren womb, even more useless than that of her mother, who at least had given birth to her.

她的丈夫恳求地吻了吻她的手。他嘴唇触碰到她肌肤的那一刻，玛丽亚浑身颤抖。

Her husband kissed her hands, pleadingly. The touch of his lips on her skin sent shivers through Maria.

我会说服议会。在这场磨难中，你不会孤军奋战。

—I will convince parliament. You will not be alone in this ordeal.

“我亲爱的……”他感激地说。

"My beloved…" he said in gratitude.

她闭上双眼，努力让自己相信那些她明知是谎言的话。可惜的是，费利佩的冷漠并没有浇灭她内心的悸动；恰恰相反，她的心跳似乎越是得不到回应，就越是急促。

She closed her eyes and tried to believe those words she knew were false. Unfortunately for her, Felipe's disinterest hadn't extinguished her own; quite the contrary, her heart seemed to beat more urgently the less reciprocated her feelings were.

 

 

 

 

在尤斯特，查尔斯祈祷儿子所面临的危险能够圆满结束。此事令他忧心忡忡，但修道院与世隔绝，这减轻了他们所听到的消息带来的冲击。日子一天天过去，午餐、诵经、祈祷和静谧的消遣——钟表，总是钟表；查尔斯的房间里很快就摆满了钟表——所有这一切都伴随着神圣的音乐。

In Yuste, Charles prayed that the danger his son faced would end happily. The matter worried him, but the monastery lived apart from the world, and this softened the impact of the news that reached them. The days passed as a succession of lunches, readings, prayers, and quiet pastimes—clocks, always clocks; Charles's chamber was soon filled with them—all accompanied by sacred music.

尽管他享受独处，这位来自根特的男士仍想利用空闲时间来维系与家人的关系，这是多年公职生涯让他无暇顾及的。家人以及照顾他们，成了他摆脱孤独的唯一途径。他还有债务要偿还，甚至还有一些人他仍然想见。

Although he enjoyed solitude, the man from Ghent wanted to use his free time to nurture his relationships with his family, something his years in office had prevented him from doing. His family, and caring for them, had become the only thing capable of pulling him out of his isolation. There were still debts to settle, and even people he still wanted to meet.

自从十年前得知儿子有了继承人后，查理就一直渴望见到他。首先，因为他是自己的亲生骨肉；其次，尽管他一向低调，但他深知自己掌握着丰富的权力运作经验；如果剥夺未来将继承菲利普王位的人学习这些经验的权利，岂不是荒谬至极？他自怜自艾：他所做的，不过是所有老年人都会做的事——努力让自己感觉有用，即使他们早已失去了作用。

Ever since he learned, a decade earlier, that his son had an heir, Charles had longed to meet him. First, because he was his own flesh and blood, and second, because, although he enjoyed downplaying his own importance, he was aware that he possessed a wealth of knowledge about the exercise of power; it seemed absurd to deny those lessons to the one who would one day succeed Philip. He pitied himself: he was doing nothing more than what all old people do, striving to feel useful even though they are no longer so.

 

 

 

 

卡洛斯王子觐见祖父时，在门口深深鞠了一躬。引他入室的弗朗西斯科·德·博尔哈鼓励孩子上前觐见这位前凯撒。孩子朝他走去。他步履间略有不稳，几乎难以察觉，但主人立刻注意到了。主人接着观察到，这孩子身体有些畸形：双肩不齐，五官也略显怪异。卡洛斯对他心生怜悯。

When Prince Carlos appeared before his grandfather, he bowed heavily at the door. Francisco de Borja, who had shown him the way to the chamber, encouraged the boy to approach the former Caesar. The child walked toward him. There was a slight, almost imperceptible irregularity in his gait, which his host noticed immediately. He then observed that the boy had a subtly deformed body: his shoulders were uneven, and, in general, his features were somewhat unusual. Carlos took pity on him.

——我的孙子兼继承人。终于！

—My grandson and heir. Finally!

男孩走上前去拥抱他。然后他们四目相对。

The boy approached to hug him. Then they looked at each other.

“你这住处真偏僻啊。”男孩说。

—This dwelling of yours is very remote—said the boy.

—这正是我欣赏她的地方。

—That's exactly what pleases me about her.

王子睁大眼睛盯着查尔斯。

The prince stared at Charles with wide eyes.

我的结局不会像你一样。上帝想让我待在宫殿里。

—The end of my days will not be like yours. God wanted me in a palace.

他的祖父笑了。

His grandfather laughed.

“如果你愿意，我鼓励你这样做。我毫不怀疑你会在各方面都比我更优秀，甚至比你的父亲更优秀。超越前人是每个人的责任。”

"If that pleases you, I encourage you to do so. I have no doubt that you will be better than me in every way, and even better than your father. It is every man's duty to surpass those who came before him."

男孩转向正在目睹这一幕的弗朗西斯科·德·博尔哈。

The boy turned to Francisco de Borja, who was witnessing the scene.

“给我拿个座位来！”他粗鲁地冲着牧师吼道。

"Bring me a seat!" he snapped rudely at the clergyman.

卡洛斯一脸茫然。

Carlos reacted with bewilderment.

—对待一个多年来一直为你服务的人，这种做法太苛刻了。

—Harsh way of treating someone who has done nothing but serve you for years.

孩子的眼神中流露出真正的惊讶：他不明白这责备是什么意思。

The child's gaze reflected genuine astonishment: he did not understand the reproach.

——就像我对待自己一样。

—As I have treated myself.

他的祖父原本希望这只是孩子任性的一时冲动，但这次探访持续的时间足以让他的希望落空。这孩子性情反复无常，举止有时甚至像个野蛮人。查理试图让他听听自己作为统治者的冒险故事，但这孩子根本听不进去。他鄙视祖父想送给他的那本关于尤利乌斯·凯撒的书，并反复念叨着荣耀这个话题——尽管这种荣耀让他误入歧途，却也让他着迷。

His grandfather wanted to believe that this whim was nothing more than a childish outburst, but the visit lasted long enough for that hope to prove false. The boy had an unpredictable temperament, and his manners, at times, resembled those of a savage. Charles tried to get him to listen to the tale of his adventures as ruler, but the child had no patience for lessons. He scorned the book about Julius Caesar that his grandfather wanted to give him and insisted repeatedly on the subject of glory, which obsessed him, albeit in a misguided way.

“你逃离了因斯布鲁克？！”他厉声问道。

"Did you flee Innsbruck?!" he spat out the question.

“我没有帮手。我们孤立无援，手无寸铁，被诸侯的军队包围着……”根特亲王从未想过自己有一天会向一个孩子解释自己的所作所为。

"I had no help. We were alone, unarmed, surrounded by the armies of the princes..." The Prince of Ghent never thought he would have to justify himself to a child.

我绝不会逃跑！绝不！

—I will never run away! Never!

男孩把失望发泄在爷爷桌上的地图上，爷爷曾徒劳地试图用这些地图教他认字。

The boy took out his disappointment on the maps his grandfather had on his desk, maps with which he had tried to teach him, in vain.

—要么我赢，要么我死！

—I would have won or I would have died!

卡洛斯亲眼看到那男孩拿起那本《凯撒回忆录》扔了出去。书页摊开，笨拙地落在地上。弗朗西斯科·德·博尔哈走上前去捡起书，递给了老人。两人交换了一个敷衍的眼神，而男孩则在他们身后继续咆哮。

Then Carlos witnessed the boy take the volume of Julius Caesar's memoirs and throw it away. The book landed awkwardly, its pages open. Francisco de Borja approached to pick it up and handed it to the old man. They exchanged a perfunctory glance, while the boy, behind them, continued to roar.

 

 

 

 

唐·卡洛斯令他的祖父失望至极，这让他陷入了悲观之中。费利佩作为他的继任者无疑是件好事，但想到这个魔鬼会接替他的位置，就令人沮丧不已。为了确保未来，他们付出了那么多努力，但从长远来看，等待他们的似乎只有混乱。

The disappointment that Don Carlos represented for his grandfather plunged him into pessimism. Having Felipe as his successor was undoubtedly a blessing, but knowing that this devil would follow him was disheartening. So much effort had been put into securing the future, and it seemed that chaos awaited in the long run.

根特亲王试图用另一件家事来缓解自己的沮丧。他的妹妹埃莉诺请求他帮忙，以便她能从葡萄牙王国获得与女儿团聚的许可。菲利普与玛丽亚公主的婚约解除——事实上，正是他一手促成了此事，因为他一心想把儿子推向英格兰——这彻底粉碎了埃莉诺与独生女重聚的希望。尽管遭遇了如此挫折，她也很快恢复过来——毕竟，命运的打击对她来说早已习以为常——但她还是决定在死前实现自己的愿望。她清楚地意识到，与女儿相见——仅此而已——便足以弥补她一生中无数的苦难。

The prince of Ghent tried to alleviate his despondency with another family matter. His sister, Eleanor, had asked him to intervene so that she could obtain permission from the Kingdom of Portugal to live with her daughter. The breaking of the engagement between Philip and the Infanta Maria, which he himself had in fact provoked by pushing his son towards England, had shattered Eleanor's hopes of being reunited with her only child. Despite this setback, from which she recovered—for if there was one thing she was accustomed to, it was the blows of fate—she had decided to fulfill her wish before death claimed her. She clearly perceived that meeting her daughter—and nothing more—would compensate her for the countless sorrows that had marked her life.

 

 

 

 

说实话，这个请求在葡萄牙宫廷引起了不安。王后凯瑟琳在托尔德西拉斯战役后的生活比她的兄弟姐妹们要舒适得多，她知道丈夫约翰和埃莉诺曾经有过一段情。埃莉诺想要回到里斯本的愿望令她感到不安：昔日的恋人从来都不是独自一人回来的，他们总是会唤起爱过他们的人的回忆。但她也对玛丽亚感到不满，玛丽亚被她视为自己的亲生母亲，却从未考虑过与她重聚的可能性。

To tell the truth, the request was met with unease at the Portuguese court. Catherine, the queen, whose life after Tordesillas had been more pleasant than that of her siblings, knew of the affair that had once taken place between her husband, John, and Eleanor. Eleanor's desire to return to Lisbon troubled her: former lovers never arrive alone, but rather with the power to stir up memories in those who had loved them. But she was also displeased that Maria, whom she considered her de facto mother, didn't even consider the possibility of reuniting with Eleanor.

“你是我的母亲，”他曾对卡塔琳娜说，“我和那个女人没有任何关系。”

"You are my mother," he had told Catalina. "I have nothing to do with that woman."

尽管法庭承诺尊重这位年轻女子的意愿，但事实上，是她母亲的恳求打动了他们。多年来，他们每月都会收到埃莉诺的来信，但这些信一到女儿手中，就被撕碎扔进了火里。

Although the court promised to respect the young woman's wishes, the truth was that her mother's plea moved them. Month after month, for years, they had received Eleanor's letters, which as soon as they reached her daughter's hands were torn up and thrown into the fire.

 

 

 

 

约翰国王大约在那时染病，最终不治身亡。当他的女儿玛丽前来送别时，他握住她的手，请求她遵从母亲的遗愿。一次会面就足够了，足以让她的灵魂得到安宁。死神近在咫尺，约翰理解了埃莉诺的痛苦：害怕临终前得不到宽恕。他自己也曾对昔日的情人有过同样的感受。在临终前的沉思和回忆中，这位君主发现自己一直在想念查理的妹妹。尽管凯瑟琳是一位无可挑剔的妻子，但约翰始终无法对她产生像对埃莉诺那样炽热的激情。与埃莉诺的决裂如此突然、如此残酷，如此不配他们曾经拥有的爱情，以至于现在为她求情似乎成了他摆脱罪恶感的唯一途径。

King John fell ill around that time, and his illness proved fatal. When his daughter Mary came to see him off at his deathbed, he took her hand and asked her to honor her mother's wishes. A single meeting would suffice; it would bring peace to her soul. Closely watched by death, John understood the anguish Eleanor carried: the fear of dying without having received forgiveness. He felt it himself regarding his former lover. In that moment of reflection and remembrance that comes on the eve of death, the monarch found himself thinking, and quite a bit, about Charles's sister. Although Catherine had been an impeccable wife, John had never been able to feel for her a passion similar to his former one. The break with Eleanor had been so abrupt, so cruel, so unworthy of the love they had shared, that interceding for her now seemed to him the only way to free himself from guilt.

玛丽亚默默地听着父亲的遗愿。此刻她内心无比煎熬，对莱昂诺尔的怨恨似乎都变得无关紧要了。国王临终前不久，她答应服从父亲的命令。

Maria listened silently to her father's wish. Torn apart as she was at that moment, the resentment she felt towards Leonor seemed dispensable and, shortly before the king died, she promised to obey him.

 

 

 

 

卡洛斯也为妹妹因女儿而承受的痛苦而感到心痛，这触动了他心中长久以来一直萦绕却又迟迟不敢触及的念头。菲利普的孩子带给他的失望让他确信，或许是时候去见见那个女人的儿子了。在德国，那个女人曾徒劳地试图让他忘记对伊莎贝拉的思念；那个女人在他面前因酒精而逐渐消逝，他对她的记忆也仅限于她甜美的歌声和她虔诚热情的片段。在那次短暂的邂逅之后的九个月里，芭芭拉·布隆伯格生下了一个儿子，不久便在母亲的祝福下被送往西班牙，以便王室能够保守当时皇帝的秘密，并为他找到一个归宿。这个金发碧眼、聪颖过人的男孩是查理的儿子，这个秘密只有三个人知道：男孩的母亲、那位来自根特的男人，以及皇帝的管家路易斯·德·基哈达。后者将孩子托付给了宫廷乐师弗朗西斯科·马西，马西和妻子并不知道孩子的身世，便在莱加内斯抚养他长大。八岁时，基哈达亲自收养了他，并负责他的教育。查理从管家那里得知了杰罗明的遭遇和境况——因为那是孩子的名字。但突然间，他渴望了解更多：他想见见这个孩子。

Carlos, too, felt touched by his sister's suffering regarding her daughter, and it stirred a thought he had long harbored but hesitated to consider. The disappointment Philip's offspring had caused him convinced him that perhaps the time had come to meet the son of the woman who, in Germany, had tried in vain to make him forget his longing for Isabella; the woman who had faded before him under the influence of alcohol, and of whom he remembered little more than her melodious singing and fragments of her pious passion. For nine months after that fleeting encounter, Barbara Blomberg had given birth to a son, who was soon sent to Spain with his mother's blessing, so that the Crown could safeguard the secret of the then-emperor and find him a home. That the blond, exceptionally bright boy was the son of Charles was a secret known only to three people: the boy's mother, the man from Ghent, and Luis de Quijada, the emperor's steward. The latter had entrusted the child to Francisco Massy, ​​a musician at the imperial court, who, along with his wife and unaware of the boy's lineage, raised him in Leganés. At the age of eight, Quijada himself took him in and assumed responsibility for his education. Charles had been informed by his steward of Jeromín's fate and circumstances—for that was the boy's name. But suddenly, he felt a desire to know more: he wanted to meet him.

于是，弗朗西斯·博尔吉亚成了他的同谋。他的主人不得不向他坦白自己与那位德国女子的风流韵事，而老人至今仍为此悔恨不已。耶稣会士被查尔斯对伊莎贝拉的忠诚所感动；这与他当时依然怀有的忠诚如出一辙。他有时觉得，两个曾深爱着她的人如今竟如此频繁地交谈、祈祷、建立友谊，却又都沉浸在永恒的哀悼之中，这真是奇妙。在不止一次的对话中，这位来自根特的男子始终能感受到博尔吉亚的情感，这一点显而易见。她的离去，让他们共同拥有彼此渴望的对象，共同承受失去她的痛苦，这反而让他们更加紧密地联系在一起，而非彼此疏远——而疏远本身也微不足道。

So Francis Borgia became his accomplice. His master had to confess to him the amorous escapade he'd had with the German woman, which the old man still regretted. The Jesuit was touched by Charles's loyalty to Isabella; it was identical to the loyalty he still felt then. It was curious, he sometimes thought, that the two men who had loved her most now shared so many conversations and prayers, friendships, and both were in eternal mourning. That the man from Ghent had always sensed Borgia's feelings became clear in more than one dialogue. With her gone, sharing the object of their desire and suffering her absence united them far more than it divided them, which was nothing.

 

 

 

 

卡洛斯王子来访时发生的一幕，在杰罗明来访时再次上演：根特亲王注视着一个同样十岁的男孩怯生生地走进他的房间。他的衣着虽然端庄，却比菲利普的儿子朴素得多；但真正让两个男孩一眼就区别开来的，是他们的体格。杰罗明优雅至极，宛如一位迷你骑士。他拥有一头美丽的金色头发和精致的五官，让卡洛斯想起了自己的母亲。与那位贫穷而又被魔法迷惑的王子不同，他的身材匀称完美。

The scene that had unfolded with the Infante Don Carlos was repeated with Jeromín's visit: the Prince of Ghent watched as a boy, also ten years old, timidly entered his chamber. His clothes, though dignified, were more humble than those of Philip's son; but what truly distinguished the two boys at first glance was their physique. Jeromín was the epitome of elegance. He looked like a miniature knight. He possessed beautiful blond hair and exquisite features that reminded Carlos of his mother. His body, unlike that of the poor, bewitched Infante, was a model of symmetry.

这种完美让他的父亲起了疑心。上帝常常用某种美德的缺失来弥补某种美德的过剩。

Such perfection made his father suspicious. God often compensated for an excess of one virtue with a lack of others.

寒暄过后，男孩怯生生地探头看向老人的桌子。桌子上摆着无数的金属制品。

After the customary greetings, the boy timidly peered over the old man's table. Countless pieces of metal rested on it.

“你喜欢手表吗？”卡洛斯问她。

—Do you like watches? —Carlos asked her.

男孩耸了耸肩。

The boy shrugged.

“我觉得我不需要它们。”他看了看另一个人。“我要去当兵。”

"I don't think I need them." He looked at the other man. "I'm going to be a soldier."

——那么，你为了实现这样的目标做了什么？你会去读那些伟大将领的传记吗？

—And what do you do to achieve such a goal? Do you read the great soldiers?

陛下，我家会读圣徒传记。

—In my house we read lives of saints, Your Majesty.

卡洛斯笑了。

Carlos smiled.

—这类阅读绝非坏事。虽然……

—Those kinds of readings are never a bad thing. Although…

他父亲把那本尤利乌斯·凯撒的回忆录递给他，那是男孩来访时读得津津有味、甚至还修补过的书。孩子饶有兴致地接过书，默默地翻阅起来。卡洛斯仍然不知道该如何看待他。

His father handed him the copy of Julius Caesar's memoirs that the boy had so thoroughly devoured during his visit, and which he had had to have mended. The child took it with interest and leafed through it in silence. Carlos still didn't know what to think of him.

把他带走。我先告辞了。

—Take him away. I excuse you now.

你为什么给我打电话？

—Why did you call me?

来自根特的男子掩饰住了自己的犹豫。

The man from Ghent concealed his hesitation.

—我想你让我想起了我的儿子。

—I suppose you remind me of my son.

杰罗明昂首挺胸，神情骄傲。随后，他神情严肃起来，喃喃自语道：

Jeromín stood tall and proud. Then he became serious and dreamed aloud:

我真希望能在你们对抗法国的斗争中帮上忙……

—I wish I could be of service to you in your fight against the French…

——时间会来的。如果说我们不缺什么，那就是与他们作战的动力。

—There will be time. If there's one thing we don't lack, it's battles against them.

男孩转身走向门口时，卡洛斯笑了。但下午又给他带来了另一个惊喜：尤斯特收到消息，他的儿子在圣康坦击败了法军。

As the boy turned his back on him and walked toward the door, Carlos smiled. But the afternoon held another happy surprise for him: news reached Yuste that his son had routed the French at Saint-Quentin.

 

 

 

 

胜利后的数日里，胜利的记忆依然萦绕在菲利普的心头——倒下的法军军旗；蒙莫朗西元帅跪在他面前；伤亡人数少得可笑，而敌军却高得离谱。他心甘情愿地沉浸在胜利的喜悦中。他父亲，伟大的凯撒的阴影，如今似乎也减轻了。

Days after the victory, memories of it continued to haunt Philip day after day—the fallen French standards; Constable Montmorency kneeling before him; the tally of casualties, ridiculously low on his side and inflated on the enemy's. Success was a state he was content to live in. The shadow of his father, the great Caesar, now seemed less heavy.

然而，令他惊讶的是，查理并没有完全消失。自从他在尤斯特隐居以来，他的父亲第一次给他寄来一封信，就如何应对胜利提出了建议。这封信的突然出现伤了菲利普的自尊心，他只读了第一段。难道他不相信查理有能力英明领导吗？查理有自己的判断力，正是这种判断力让他取得了对法国的辉煌胜利。至于他身边的人是否认同他的想法，那就是另一回事了。

However, to his surprise, Charles hadn't disappeared entirely. For the first time since his seclusion at Yuste, his father sent him a letter with advice on how to manage his victory. This intrusion wounded Philip's pride, and he read only the first paragraph. Did he not believe him capable of leading wisely? He possessed his own judgment, the same judgment that had led him to such a resounding triumph over France. Whether those around him agreed with his ideas was another matter.

 

 

 

 

—我们接下来去巴黎吧。

—Let's move on to Paris.

在英国宫廷的议事厅里，格兰维尔红衣主教和阿尔巴公爵听了国王的话后，交换了一个困惑的眼神。

In the council chamber of the English court, Cardinal Granvelle and the Duke of Alba, after hearing the king's words, exchanged a look of bewilderment.

“为什么？”牧师问道，“圣康坦战役的胜利已经非常辉煌了。你们不会打算吞并法国吧？”

"Why?" the clergyman inquired. "The victory at Saint-Quentin has already been overwhelming. You don't intend to annex France, do you?"

“即便不能吞并，至少也要威慑他们，让他们投降的条件对我来说无可挑剔。这并非痴人说梦；英格兰和我的联合军队完全有能力让这座城市屈服！”

"If not annexation, at least let's intimidate them enough to make the terms of their surrender unbeatable for me. It's not a pipe dream; England and my united troops can very well bring the city to its knees!"

菲利普按照惯例征求了公爵的意见，但公爵保持沉默，目光始终盯着他们所在的大陆地图。

Philip, as was his custom, sought the opinion of the duke, who remained silent, his gaze fixed on the map of the continent around which they were located.

——或许亨利会决定调动驻扎在意大利的军队来对付我们。我们会被卷入交火之中。

—Perhaps Henry would then decide to unleash the troops he has stationed in Italy against us. We would be caught in the crossfire.

国王看着地图，设想了这种可能性。

The king, also looking at the map, imagined that contingency.

但我们必须采取措施巩固胜利。如果不是巴黎，告诉我，是哪个城市？

—But we must do something to consolidate our victory. If not Paris, tell me, what city?

“殿下，”格兰维拉回答说，“这场斗争不会给你带来比它已经带给你的更多。庆祝你已经取得的成就吧，因为这已经非常了不起了。”

"Your Highness," Granvela replied, "you will gain nothing more from this struggle than what it has already given you. Celebrate what you have achieved, for it is already a great deal."

阿尔瓦公爵没有反驳红衣主教。菲利普感到沮丧，折起地图，结束了会面。他不想成为那种凭着神启和自负混杂的头脑做决定的君主。作为西班牙摄政王，他曾饱受父亲反复无常的对法战争之苦，他信奉精于算计；野心并未蒙蔽他的双眼。

The Duke of Alba did not refute the cardinal. Frustrated, Philip folded the map and ended the meeting. He did not wish to be one of those monarchs who made decisions based on a mixture of divine inspiration and egomania. As regent of Spain, he had suffered through his father's capricious wars against the French, and he believed in calculation; ambition did not blind him.

然而，他似乎并不确信。对他而言，圣昆廷之战的胜利虽然辉煌，却既不够，也未能给他带来信心。

And yet, he didn't seem convinced. For him, the victory in San Quintín, although magnificent, was neither enough nor did it give him confidence.

 

 

 

 

杰罗明把《高卢战记》送给了卡洛斯。

Jeromín gave Carlos the copy of The Gallic Wars .

“你已经读过了？”凯撒问道，语气中既有惊讶又有怀疑。

—Have you already read it? —said Caesar, somewhere between astonished and skeptical.

——是的，陛下。

—Yes, Your Majesty.

—你最喜欢哪一段？

—Which passage did you like the most?

男孩沉思着。维拉的阳光伴着他们散步。这天阳光灿烂，只有偶尔飞来的蚊子令人烦恼。卡洛斯走得很艰难：痛风发作，丝毫没有缓解的迹象，而事实上，他也没有采取任何措施来控制病情。他屡次无视医生让他戒肉戒酒的建议。他觉得生命所剩无几，不能剥夺自己仅存的几分乐趣。

The boy pondered it. The Vera sun accompanied them on their walk. The day was magnificent; only the occasional mosquito was a nuisance. Carlos walked with difficulty: his gout gave him no respite, and the truth was, he did nothing to stop it. He repeatedly ignored the doctors' advice to abstain from meat and beer. He had too little life left to deprive himself of the few pleasures available to him.

“我喜欢凯撒在战前向军队发表讲话。当士兵们相信他们的领袖时，没有什么能阻止他们，”他若有所思地说。

"I like it when the Caesar addresses his armies before battle. When soldiers believe in their leader, nothing can stop them," he stated thoughtfully.

卡洛斯惊奇地凝视着他。潺潺溪流声暂时盖过了他们的谈话。

Carlos gazed at him in wonder. The murmur of a stream monopolized the conversation for a moment.

—如果你已经明白这一点，那么关于战争你只需要再明白一个真相：你不可能永远获胜。根据具体情况，撤退是一种需要勇气的行为。

—If you already know that, there's only one more truth about war you need to learn: that you can't always win. Retreating, depending on the circumstances, is an act that requires courage.

他们说你逃走了。在德国。

—They say you fled. In Germany.

来自根特的男子放慢了脚步。

The man from Ghent slowed his steps.

—你对此有何看法？

—And what do you think of that?

“我想仔细考虑一下我的答案，”男孩回答道。

"I'd like to think carefully about my answer," the boy replied.

杰罗明因为没有得到答案而感到困惑，但事实上，他仍然难以自信地表达自己的想法。他常常一会儿持有一种观点，过不了多久又会改变主意。在他看来，生活远比一些人想象的要复杂得多。他不知道的是，卡洛斯认为这种疑虑远比任何确定性都更有洞察力，他从杰罗明身上看到了自己的影子，比以往任何时候都更像自己的亲生儿子。

Jeromín felt bewildered at not receiving an answer, but the truth was that he still struggled to speak with certainty. Often he would hold one opinion, and then a short while later, the opposite. Life seemed more complex to him than some people believed. What he didn't know was that Carlos found this doubt far more insightful than any certainty, and that he recognized himself in Jeromín and felt him more like his own son than ever before.

在下次拜访老人时，他解答了老人的问题。

It was on his next visit to the old man that he answered his question.

—如果你让自己被俘虏，你就不是一个合格的将军。

—You would have been a bad general if you had let yourselves be captured.

他父亲笑了。那次他们在卧室见面：卡洛斯太虚弱了，无法出门。

His father smiled. On that occasion they met in the bedroom: Carlos was too weak to venture outside.

那个来自根特的人递给他一本书。他接过书，看了看书脊，毫不掩饰自己的失望。那是《高卢战记》的第二卷。

The man from Ghent handed him a book. Upon taking it and reading the spine, he made no secret of his disappointment. It was the second volume of The Gallic Wars .

我以为你喜欢呢。

—I thought you liked it.

——陛下，我更想读您的回忆录。

—I would prefer to read your memoirs, Your Majesty.

卡洛斯掩饰了自己的情绪。他转移话题，以免暴露自己的爱意，也避免暴露他们之间关系的真相。

Carlos concealed his emotion. He changed the subject to avoid revealing his affection and, with it, the truth about their relationship.

—你问过谁关于因斯布鲁克发生的事情？你父亲吗？

—Who did you ask about what happened in Innsbruck? Your father?

“什么父亲？”这个回答让来自根特的男子震惊不已。“奎哈达照顾我，但他不是我的父亲。”

"What father?" The reply shocked the man from Ghent. "Quijada takes care of me, but he isn't my father."

你是如何得出这个结论的？

—How did you reach that conclusion?

“他是个有荣誉感的人。如果他是我的父亲，他绝不会把我托付给另一个家庭照顾这么多年。任何一个有荣誉感的人都不会这样做。”

"He's a man of honor. He wouldn't have left me in the care of another family for years if he had been my father. No man of honor would do that."

卡洛斯从未像遭受那样被战争创伤所撕裂。

No war wound had ever lacerated Carlos like that response.

 

 

 

 

玛丽亚与哥哥卡洛斯重逢时，他热情地迎接了她。他带她参观了自己的房间，以及最近几天新装的钟表。钟表的滴答声令她感到悲伤：这似乎预示着他身体的迅速衰弱，因为她发现他时，他的健康状况已经很差了。她刚从葡萄牙回来，之前她陪同玛丽亚公主前往卡斯蒂利亚与母亲见面。但公主并没有和她同行。

When Maria was reunited with her brother Carlos, he greeted her with genuine affection. He showed her his rooms and the clocks he had installed in recent days. The ticking of the devices saddened her: they seemed to mark his rapid decline, as she had found him in poor health. She was returning from Portugal, where she had traveled to accompany the Infanta Maria to Castile for her meeting with her mother. But the young woman was not with her.

他选择违背对父亲的誓言。他说既然已经有了房子，就不想再去找房子了。

—He has chosen to break his oath to his father. He says he doesn't want to look for homes now that he already has one.

卡洛斯悲痛地听到了这个消息。

Carlos received the news with sorrow.

可怜的莱昂诺尔……她知道了吗？

—Poor Leonor… Does she know yet?

玛丽亚点了点头。从她的表情来看，很明显，这个消息对她的另一个妹妹产生了怎样的影响。

Maria nodded. Judging by her expression, it was clear how the news had affected her other sister.

“这件事我连让她满意都没能做到。”卡洛斯叹息着，颓然地瘫坐在椅子上。“又一次失败，真是雪上加霜。”

—I haven't even been able to please her on this matter— Carlos lamented as he slumped into his chair. —Another failure to add to so many.

她握住他的手，带着温柔的责备看着他。

She took his hand and looked at him with tender reproach.

-“失败”…

-"Failure"…

—当一个人取得的成就与他所渴望的完全不同时，你会如何称呼这种情况？

—What do you call it when what one achieves bears no resemblance to what one aspired to?

“如果你无法控制改革者，那是因为教会没有给你任何帮助。或许你太过理想化，以为自己可以独自应对一切。失望并非源于我们最终得到的，而是源于我们原本想要得到的……”

"If you couldn't contain the reformers, it was because the Church offered you no help. Perhaps you were idealistic to think you could handle it all alone. Disappointment doesn't come from what we get, but from what we intended to get..."

“我本可以把他彻底铲除！”卡洛斯痛苦地打断道，“我放过了路德，玛丽亚。”

"It was within my power to cut him off at the root!" Carlos interrupted, tormented. "I let Luther escape alive, Maria."

—为过去的事情担忧有什么用呢？

—What's the point of worrying about what's already in the past?

“未来更让我担忧。我的孙子……”她说着，选择了沉默。

"The future worries me even more. My grandson..." she said, choosing to remain silent.

——你的人民会找到出路，就像你一样。相信，哪怕只有一次。

—Your people will find a way, just like you. Trust, even if it's just for once.

——如果还有另一个孩子呢？一个罪孽深重的孩子，却才华横溢，品格高尚……

—And what if there were another child? A child of sin, but brilliant and with the character one should have…

玛丽亚很惊讶，但她不想从他口中套出什么话。

Maria was surprised, but she didn't want to pry anything out of him.

你会知道如何做出正确的决定。如果你后悔路德的遭遇，那就说明你已经吸取了教训。要用你的智慧来判断。

—You will know how to make the right decision. If you regret what happened with Luther, it means you have learned. Judge with your wisdom.

卡洛斯紧紧抓住她的手。

Carlos clung to her hand.

—你比我更适合当皇后，我更适合当皇帝。

—You would have been a better empress than I would have been emperor.

我师从最优秀的人。

—I learned from the best.

玛丽亚该离开的时间到了。她们拥抱告别，并约定下次再见，尽管她们谁也无法否认，那一刻或许已经太迟了。

It was the appointed time for Maria to leave. They hugged and made plans to meet again, although neither of them could deny that that moment might come too late.

 

 

 

 

莱昂诺尔在一个冬日的清晨，在巴达霍斯的一栋别墅里去世了。她一直待在边境附近，仿佛不愿接受再也见不到女儿的残酷现实。每当她听到家附近传来马蹄声，她都会向窗外望去，然后再次失望而归。

Leonor died one winter morning in a villa in Badajoz. She had remained near the border, as if she refused to accept that she would never see her daughter again. Whenever she heard horses' hooves near her home, she would look out the window and be disappointed once more.

得知玛丽亚公主的决定后，莱昂诺尔哭了数日，渐渐地，她的身体每况愈下。那天早晨，她没有试图阻止死亡的到来，便已做好了赴死的准备。她没有任何美好的回忆可以带走，就连与葡萄牙国王约翰的幸福也变得毫无意义，因为他夺走的女儿立刻浮现在她的脑海。于是，她轻轻地沉入了梦乡。她感到一种平静：她再也不用面对皇帝的意志、傲慢的国王，以及那些并非毫无道理地疏远她的女儿们。虚无似乎成了一张舒适的床，让她可以安然入睡。

After weeping for days upon learning of Princess Maria's decision, Leonor faded away. Her body steadily deteriorated, and without trying to prevent it, she found herself ready to die that morning. She had no sweet memories to take with her, for not even her happiness with John of Portugal held any value, as the daughter he had taken from her immediately came to mind. So she simply drifted off to sleep, gently. And she felt a sense of peace: she would no longer have to face the will of emperors, disdainful kings, or daughters who, not without reason, shunned her. Nothingness seemed a comfortable bed in which to lie down.

当她的意识几乎完全消散时，她感觉到了什么：胸腔里微弱的心跳声。伴着这节奏，莱昂诺尔离开了这个世界。

When her consciousness had almost completely faded, she felt something: those small heartbeats in her chest. To the rhythm they played, Leonor left this world.

 

 

 

 

与此同时，在英国宫廷里，一个名字被反复提及，语气中带着一丝不安，仿佛有人要说魔鬼的坏话：加莱。法国人在圣康坦战役战败后重整旗鼓，而这座要塞正是他们的战利品。他们发动了唯一一次能够造成最大破坏的打击，因为加莱此前一直是英国的领地。通过这次征服，他们不仅收复了在圣康坦失去的一切，还让腓力二世为英国遭受的惨重损失承担了责任。

Meanwhile, at the English court, one name was repeated with the apprehension of someone who would speak ill of the devil: Calais. The French had regrouped after their defeat at Saint-Quentin, and this stronghold had been their prize. They had struck the only blow they could deliver where it would cause the most damage, for Calais was, until then, an English possession. With this conquest, they not only returned what they had received at Saint-Quentin, but also made Philip responsible for what was a terrible loss for the British.

查理的儿子对发生的一切怒不可遏。他是对的：一场胜利远远不够，而且根本没人支持他！此时此刻，他本该身在巴黎，率领着经验丰富的方阵、意大利军队和英国军队，在灰蒙蒙的冬日天空下高举利剑，宣告自己是法兰西的统治者。他多么天真，竟然相信别人的判断，而他早已明白，只有自己的判断才能指引他；他自己的……以及他父亲的判断。意识到这一点后，菲利普立刻拿起了尤斯特不久前寄来的那封信。他焦急地展开信纸，迫不及待地读了起来。

Charles's son reacted to what had happened with fury. He had been right: one victory wasn't enough, and no one had backed him up! By now he should have been in Paris, at the head of the veteran tercios, the Italian troops, and the English, raising his sword to the gray winter sky and proclaiming himself master of France. How naive he had been to trust the judgment of others, when he had learned that only his own would guide him; his own… and his father's. When he realized this, Philip pounced on the letter that had arrived some time ago from Yuste. He unfolded it before him anxiously, and read it with the same eagerness.

 

 

……我的孩子，不要沉浸在圣康坦战役的胜利光环中。法国永远不会屈服，宁愿战死也不愿让你功亏一篑。如今你已是英格兰国王，听听我这个可怜老人的忠告：务必守住加莱。

…Do not rest on the laurels of the victory at Saint-Quentin, my son. France always responds, and would rather die than leave you victorious. Now that you are King of the English, listen to this poor old man who tells you: take care of Calais.

 

 

费利佩跪倒在办公室里。他闭上眼睛，暗自咒骂自己。他想起很久以前的想法，那时卡洛斯还在位高权重，而他作为继承人一心想接班。那时，他坚信自己会在各方面都超越年迈的父亲。然而现在，他却严重怀疑自己是否真的能够成功。

Felipe fell to his knees in his office. He closed his eyes and cursed himself. He remembered what he had thought long ago, when Carlos still held power and he was an heir eager to succeed him. Back then, he had been convinced that he would improve upon his aging father in every way. Now, however, he had serious doubts that he would ever succeed.

 

 

 

 

九月的一个午后，查尔斯在阳光下休息，鸟儿在寂静的夜色中鸣叫，他感到一阵不适。他感到一阵闷热难耐。他意识到自己在户外待的时间太长了，便叫人送他回住处。回到住处后，他头痛欲裂。他躺到床上睡着了。醒来时，他浑身是汗，还感到一阵恶心。医生们赶来为他诊治。检查之后，他们问他前几天是否被蚊子叮咬过。查尔斯点点头：他喜欢去修道院附近的小溪，那里蚊子经常出没。医生们的表情从怀疑转为担忧。

One September afternoon, while resting in the sun—the birds chirping for him against a backdrop of perfect silence—Charles felt unwell. The sensation was one of stifling heat. He deduced that he had already spent too many hours outdoors and sent for help to return to his quarters. Once there, a headache struck. He lay down on his bed and fell asleep. When he awoke, his body was bathed in sweat, and he felt nauseous. The physicians came to his aid. After examining him, they asked if he had been bitten by any mosquitoes in the preceding days. Charles nodded: he liked the stream near the monastery, and those insects often thrived there. The doctors' expressions shifted from suspicion to concern.

 

 

 

 

意识到自己时日无多，这位早已不复存在的人安排好了自己的葬礼，并尽快举行。那些服侍他的人觉得他的要求有些悲观，但卡洛斯希望能够亲眼见证自己离世后的情景。

Aware that his time had come, the man who was no longer anyone arranged for his funeral to be organized as soon as possible. Those who attended to him considered his request pessimistic, but Carlos wished to be present for a rehearsal of what would happen when he was gone.

根特人身患重病，寒意袭人，但他还是参加了自己的葬礼。葬礼简朴而庄严肃穆，令他感到欣慰。他亲自挑选的音乐，为现场增添了一丝温暖。仆人们身着丧服，扮演着前来参加葬礼的人。他们并非缺乏感情。毕竟，他们知道这场戏很快就会变成现实。

Throbbing with the chills of his illness, the man from Ghent attended his own funeral. It was a simple yet solemn affair, and it pleased him. The music, chosen by him, lent warmth to the scene. The servants, dressed in mourning, played the part of those who would attend the funeral. They were not lacking in feeling. After all, they knew that the charade would soon become reality.

查尔斯虽然发烧后感到疲惫，但心情愉悦，便回房休息。他并不惧怕死亡，只是担心死神会在他完成计划中的回忆录、努力成为一个“有荣誉感的人”之前夺走他的生命。

Pleasant and exhausted by the fever, Charles retired to rest. He had no fear of death, only that it might claim him before he finished the memoirs he had decided to write and before he had tried to become a "man of honor."

 

 

 

 

第二天，高烧让他昏昏欲睡。他心想，这样也好；他浑身酸痛。他正要打个盹，却被一个声音打断了。

The next day the fever kept him drowsy. It was better that way, he thought; his whole body ached. One of his nods was interrupted by the sound of a voice.

“形势危急。凯撒见状，拿起后方一名士兵的盾牌，走到前线。在那里，他逐一叫出百夫长的名字，与他们交谈……”

—“The situation was critical. Seeing this, Caesar took the shield of a soldier in the rear and advanced to the front line. There he spoke to each of the centurions, calling each one by name…”

杰罗明意识到卡洛斯在看着他，便停止了阅读。

Jeromín stopped reading when he realized that Carlos was looking at him.

“请您原谅我，”老人说道。

"You must forgive me," said the old man.

—大人，您这是什么意思？

—What do you mean, my lord?

他父亲的嘴唇因发烧和紧张而颤抖。

His father's lips trembled, from fever and nerves.

—我明天会回来把结局读给你听。

—I'll come back tomorrow and read you the ending.

垂死之人点了点头。在再次沉入梦乡之前，他的目光变得黯淡，与他以往看向孩子的眼神截然不同；那一刻，孩子明白了男人想要被原谅的是什么：他一直以来所怀疑的那件事。

The dying man nodded. Before falling asleep again, his gaze clouded over, unlike any he had ever given the child; at that moment the child knew what the man wanted to be forgiven for: that which he had always suspected.

 

 

 

 

当晚，弗朗西斯·博尔吉亚应召而来，发现查理面容憔悴苍白，仿佛来自另一个世界。这位耶稣会士坐在他身旁，给了查理一些时间积蓄力量开口。

——父亲，亲爱的博尔哈……我打算在我的遗嘱中添加一份附录。

—Father, dear Borja… I am going to add a codicil to my will.

牧师听了很高兴，他认为这是公正的。

The clergyman was pleased to hear it. He believed it to be just.

我会让他随我的姓，我也希望他能继承家族中一个尊贵的名字。就叫他胡安吧，以纪念我的母亲。

博尔哈点了点头。

Borja nodded.

——至于我的另一个儿子……我想给他留下一些东西。

—And to my other son… there is something I would like to bequeath to him.

 

 

 

 

黎明时分，博尔哈不得不返回主人的房间。他推开围在他身边的修士们。其中一个修士低声对他说：“他快要死了。”

At dawn, Borja had to return to his master's chamber. He pushed aside the swarm of friars who surrounded him. One of them whispered to him: "He's dying."

卡洛斯虽已奄奄一息，却仍保持清醒。他看到耶稣会士，便用慵懒的手势示意他到自己身边。博尔哈强忍着沮丧，将耳朵凑近病人的嘴边。

——皇后的十字架。

—The Empress's crucifix.

牧师深受感动，点了点头。他从桌上拿起那件自根特来人抵达尤斯特后就一直放在那里的东西，递给了查尔斯。查尔斯紧紧地抱着那件东西，亲吻了它，然后把它放在胸口。他始终没有松开它，直到死去。

Moved, the clergyman nodded. He took it from the table where it had rested since the man from Ghent arrived at Yuste and handed it to him. Charles clung to the object, kissed it, and placed it on his chest. Without letting go of it, he died.

 

 

 

 

信封封面上用手写着一行字：“致我的儿子”。费利佩震惊不已，抚摸着信件。他身着丧服，陪同他的阿尔巴公爵和格朗维尔红衣主教也同样如此。

—Go away.

其他人神色凝重地遵命而行。虽然仍是九月，但英格兰的天气已经寒冷，宫殿内也明显感受到了这一点。炉火已燃起，但菲利普却感觉不到一丝温暖。

With a grave expression, the others obeyed. It was still September, but the weather was already cold in England, and this was noticeable inside the palace. The fire was lit, but Philip felt no warmth.

他手捧着书页走向火堆。他凝视着眼前跳跃噼啪作响的火焰，仿佛在召唤着他。国王的牙齿打颤，但并非因为灼热。他怒吼一声，将手稿扔进火中。看着书页的边角燃烧，他又一次嚎叫起来。当他双手捂住脸时，声音更大了。突然，仿佛从某种魔咒中醒来，他冲到火边，救回了手稿。他用手熄灭了炉中残存的蓝色小火苗。然后，他沉浸在对父亲的回忆中：父亲的功绩、恐惧、遭受的背叛、亲人离世；所有的喜悦和痛苦；未能成为最好的兄弟、最好的儿子、最好的丈夫、最好的父亲的愧疚；荣耀、失败、青春和暮年；以及他对父亲直至生命最后一刻的爱。

He approached the fire, carrying the pages. He fixed his eyes on the flames, which danced and crackled before him, inviting. The king's teeth chattered, but not from the heat. He let out a cry of rage before throwing the manuscript into the fire. He cried out again as he watched the corners of the pages burn. And again, even louder, when he buried his face in his hands. Suddenly, as if awakening from a spell, he rushed to the fire and rescued the text. He extinguished with his hands the small blue flames that still flickered within it. He then embraced the memories of his father: his exploits, his fears, the betrayals he had suffered, the deaths that had struck him; every joy and every torment; the guilt of not having been the best brother, the best son, the best husband, or the best father; the glory, the failure, the youth, and the twilight. to the love he had felt for her until the very last day.

于是，儿子紧紧抓住父亲的生命，放声大哭。

And so, clinging to his father's life, the son burst into tears.

劳拉·萨米恩托·帕拉雷斯（1979年生于马德里）是一位编剧。她本科学习哲学，后毕业于马德里电影学院，获得编剧学位。此后，她参与创作了多部电视剧，包括《继承人》（Herederos）、《火葬场》（Crematorio）和《伊莎贝尔》（Isabel ）等。目前，她正在为电影《卡洛斯，皇帝之王》（Carlos, Rey Emperador）撰写剧本，并开发其他电影项目。

Laura Sarmiento Pallarés (Madrid, 1979) is a screenwriter. After studying Philosophy, she earned a degree in Screenwriting from the Madrid Film School. Since then, she has worked on the television series Herederos , Crematorio , and Isabel , among others. She is currently writing the screenplays for Carlos, Rey Emperador and developing film projects.
